pages.title: What this unit is about
pages.body:
> 📝 **Strand 2 — Productivity Software**
Sub-strand 4: Introduction to Electronic Spreadsheet

Spreadsheets become databases when data is well structured. In this unit you will build a class data table, validate entries, sort and filter, use styles, templates and macros, and summarise data with pivot tables and pivot charts.

pages.title: Content standard and lessons
pages.body:
> 🎯 **Content standard**
- **B9.2.4.1** Demonstrate how to use the spreadsheet (advanced operations).

> 🧭 **What you will be able to do**
- **B9.2.4.1.1** Perform data filtering, sorting and validation.
- **B9.2.4.1.2** Demonstrate how to use styles, themes, templates and macros.
- **B9.2.4.1.3** Demonstrate the use of data tables, pivot tables, charts and pivot charts.

> 🗺️ **Lessons in this unit**
- 7.1 Fields, Records, Validation, Sorting and Filtering
- 7.2 Styles, Themes, Templates and Macros
- 7.3 Data Tables, Pivot Tables, Charts and Pivot Charts

**Core competencies developed:** Communication and Collaboration (CC9.6), Digital Literacy (DL5.1), Critical Thinking (CP5.1), Creativity (CI5.4).

lessons.title: Fields, Records, Validation, Sorting and Filtering

pages.title: Fields, Records, Validation, Sorting and Filtering
pages.body:
Curriculum indicator B9.2.4.1.1
> 🎯 **Learning objectives** By the end of this lesson you should be able to:
- describe fields, records and tables;
- construct a structured data table and apply validation rules;
- convert data to a table (list), sort and filter.
| **Term** | **Meaning** | **Example** |
|---|---|---|
| Field | A **column** holding one type of data about every item | Surname, Date of Birth, Sex |
| Record | A **row** holding all the data about one item | All details of one learner |
| Structured table | Data organised in rows and columns with one heading row, one type of data per column, no blank rows | A class register |
| Unstructured data | Data with no fixed format | Essays, photos, WhatsApp chats, a page of mixed notes |
> 💻 **Practical session — Build a class data table**
In a new workbook, type the headings in row 1: **Surname, First name, Date of Birth, Sex, Home Town, Region**. Enter data for at least 15 classmates (with their permission, or use made-up data).
## Data validation
**Data validation** sets rules that control what can be entered in a cell, preventing errors.
[[fig:c9-f08|Figure 7: A validation drop-down list in the Sex column]]
> 🪜 **Step by step — Creating a validation drop-down list for Sex**
1. Select the cells in the **Sex** column (e.g. D2:D50).
2. Click **Data › Data Tools › Data Validation**.
3. On the **Settings** tab, under **Allow**, choose **List**; in **Source**, type M,F.
4. On the **Input Message** tab, type a hint such as “Choose M or F”.
5. On the **Error Alert** tab, choose **Stop** and type “Please select M or F only.” Click **OK**.
6. Click a cell in the column: a drop-down arrow appears. Typing anything else shows the error.

pages.title: Fields, Records, Validation, Sorting and Filtering (continued)
pages.body:
| **Other validation rules** | **Example** |
|---|---|
| Whole number between limits | Test score between 0 and 100 |
| Date | Date of Birth between 01/01/2008 and 31/12/2014 |
| Text length | Phone number exactly 10 characters |
| Custom formula | No duplicate index numbers |
## Converting data to a table (list)
Click any cell in the data and press **Ctrl + T** (or **Insert › Table**), confirm **My table has headers**, and click **OK**. The range becomes an Excel **Table** (called a “list” in older versions): it gets banded rows, filter arrows, automatic expansion when you add records in the next row, and a **Total Row** option (**Table Design › Total Row**). New records are entered simply by typing in the first empty row below the table.
## Sorting and filtering
> 🪜 **Step by step — Sorting and filtering**
1. Click any cell in the **Surname** column, then **Data › Sort A to Z** (ascending) or **Sort Z to A** (descending).
2. For several levels, click **Data › Sort** and add levels (e.g. by Region, then by Surname).
3. Click **Data › Filter** (or use the table’s arrows). Click the arrow on **Sex**, untick **Select All**, tick **F** and click **OK** to show only female learners.
4. Use **Text Filters**, **Number Filters** or **Date Filters** for conditions (e.g. born after 2012). Click **Clear** to show all records again.

pages.title: Styles, Themes, Templates and Macros
pages.body:
Curriculum indicator B9.2.4.1.2
> 🎯 **Learning objectives** By the end of this lesson you should be able to:
- describe the difference between templates and macros;
- create documents from templates;
- apply styles and themes; explore macros.
|  | **Template** | **Macro** |
|---|---|---|
| Meaning | A pre-designed workbook used as a **starting point** for new workbooks (layout, formulas, formats) | A **recorded set of actions or instructions** that can be run automatically to repeat a task |
| Purpose | Saves design time; gives consistent documents | Automates repetitive tasks |
| File type | .xltx (or .xltm with macros) | Stored in a macro-enabled workbook .xlsm |
| Example | Budget, invoice, attendance tracker, calendar | Format a monthly report in one click |
> 🪜 **Step by step — Creating a workbook from a template**
1. Click **File › New**.
2. Choose a featured template or search (e.g. “attendance”, “budget”, “gradebook”).
3. Click **Create**, then replace the sample data with your own and save as a normal workbook.
**Cell Styles** (Home › Styles › Cell Styles) apply ready-made formats such as Heading 1, Good, Bad, Currency and Total. **Format as Table** applies table styles. **Themes** (Page Layout › Themes) change the colours, fonts and effects of the whole workbook at once.
> 💻 **Practical session — Style project**
Format your class data table with a table style, apply the Title cell style to a heading above the table, then try three different **Themes** and choose the most readable one.

pages.title: Macros
pages.body:
## Macros
> 🪜 **Step by step — Recording a simple macro**
1. Show the **Developer** tab: **File › Options › Customise Ribbon**, tick **Developer**, click **OK**.
2. Click **Developer › Record Macro**. Name it FormatHeader (no spaces) and set a shortcut such as **Ctrl + Shift + H**. Click **OK**.
3. Perform the actions: select row 1, make it bold, fill it dark blue, change the font colour to white, and centre it.
4. Click **Developer › Stop Recording**.
5. On another sheet, press **Ctrl + Shift + H**: the macro repeats all the steps instantly.
6. Save as ∗Excel Macro-Enabled Workbook (.xlsm)∗∗.
> 🛡️ **Safety first — Macro security** Macros are written in **VBA** code, and criminals can hide malware in them. Never enable macros in files from unknown senders. By default, Office blocks macros in files downloaded from the Internet.

lessons.title: Data Tables, Pivot Tables, Charts and Pivot Charts

pages.title: Data Tables, Pivot Tables, Charts and Pivot Charts
pages.body:
Curriculum indicator B9.2.4.1.3
> 🎯 **Learning objectives** By the end of this lesson you should be able to:
- explore pivot tables and pivot charts;
- summarise the class data set;
- insert a pivot chart of males and females; sort and filter the pivot table.
A **pivot table** is an interactive tool that **summarises** large amounts of data (counting, totalling, averaging) by dragging fields into areas, without writing formulas. A **pivot chart** is a chart linked to a pivot table that updates when the pivot table changes.
[[fig:c9-f09|Figure 8: Summarising the class data with a pivot table]]
> 🪜 **Step by step — Creating a pivot table and pivot chart of males and females**
1. Click any cell in your class data table.
2. Click **Insert › PivotTable**, confirm the table/range, choose **New Worksheet**, and click **OK**.
3. In the **PivotTable Fields** pane, drag **Sex** to **Rows** and **Surname** to **Values**. Excel shows **Count of Surname** for F and M with a **Grand Total**.
4. Drag **Region** to **Columns** to see how many males and females come from each region.
5. Click inside the pivot table, then **PivotTable Analyze › PivotChart**; choose **Clustered Column** or **Pie** to display the number of males and females in the class.
6. Use the arrow beside **Row Labels** to **sort** (A to Z, or by count) and **filter** (e.g. show only one region). Add a **Slicer** (PivotTable Analyze › Insert Slicer) for click-to-filter buttons.
7. If the source data changes, click **PivotTable Analyze › Refresh**.

pages.title: Data Tables, Pivot Tables, Charts and Pivot Charts (continued)
pages.body:
> ✨ **Did you know? — What-If data tables** Excel also has a feature called a **Data Table** (**Data › What-If Analysis › Data Table**) that shows how changing one or two inputs changes a formula result, for example how monthly savings change with different interest rates. Do not confuse it with converting a range into an Excel **Table** (Ctrl + T).
Normal **charts** (Insert › Charts) are made from ordinary ranges; choose **Column** for comparisons, **Line** for trends over time, **Pie** for parts of a whole and **Bar** for long category names. Always add a chart title and axis titles.

pages.body:
> ✏️ **Review exercises** — answer these in your exercise book or on the computer, then check with your teacher.

1. Distinguish between fields and records, and between structured and unstructured data.
2. Describe how to create a validation list for the Sex column.
3. Explain the difference between a template and a macro.
